item.title: Sizing RAM and vCPU for a Local Language Model: Calculating the Initial VM Size
item.description:
Sizing RAM and vCPU for a local language model starts with specific weights and a request profile. Initial self-hosted LLM requirements include input and output length, concurrency, runtime, and offload scheme. Calculation based on weight size and KV cache formula provides an initial configuration, while a warm-up test reveals actual memory consumption and the point where CPU ceases to help. Read more

item.title: The computation race has reached mathematics
item.description:
A major breakthrough in mathematics and AI is unfolding. While the singularity is still distant, mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge have been working on the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. They achieved a significant result: finite-time blowup for forced 3D Euler equations, using AI tools like Claude and Codex, and formalizing proofs in Lean. This led to a viral rumor about Anthropic solving Millennium Prize Problems, which was inaccurate. OpenAI, however, leveraged this momentum, training a new model that reportedly tackled remaining Millennium Prize Problems, including Navier-Stokes. This article details the events, the controversy surrounding authorship and data usage, and the ethical implications for AI in research.

item.title: RAG, Search, and Long Context: Why Complex Pipelines Aren't Always Necessary
item.description:
In 2023, RAG was the only way to inject knowledge into LLMs due to small context windows and frequent hallucinations. RAG became a popular technology for natural language search over knowledge bases. However, RAG pipelines are complex and labor-intensive. Companies want chatbots for their documentation. Developers propose pipelines involving chunking, embeddings, vector databases, and re-rankers, taking months of work and ongoing maintenance for limited benefit. Today, many models support 1M+ tokens, often fitting entire documentation within their context window. But if it doesn't fit, is building a full RAG system immediately necessary? How do we know when an alternative to RAG exists? This article explores why RAG became the default choice (and why it was justified), examines quality degradation with Long Context, compares approaches, and guides on what to use and when.

item.title: Opening up Alice AI Search Pre-training: How Alice's Fast Answers Model Works in Search
item.description:
Alice AI's Fast Answer is Yandex's most massive generative product and the first touchpoint with Alice for Search users. Even during peak load, users must receive a concise answer in seconds. To achieve this, the Alice AI Search team adapts the entire fast answer pipeline—from custom architecture pre-training to online RL training on user behavioral signals. This article explains how generative answers work in Search and details the June release's main improvements: how answers were accelerated using short info-contexts, why Encoder-Decoder was combined with a sparse MoE architecture, and how training on real user signals impacted product quality and usage. Additionally, the trained Alice AI-T5-35B-A0.6B Base model is now publicly available, with inference accessible via Hugging Face Transformers, while optimized production inference remains internal to Yandex. Read on.

item.title: AI can already assemble microservices from a single prompt, but as a developer, I'm still needed
item.description:
Every few years (and now even more often), developers are buried again. First, visual builders were supposed to replace us. Then no-code. Then low-code. Then auto-generation of CRUD. Then Copilot. Now, it seems, the final boss has arrived in the form of large language models, which can whip up a backend, frontend, Docker Compose, migrations, OpenAPI, Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, authorization, tests, README, and a compiler on the side in an evening. And if you open any social network, you'll see everywhere: 'I made a SaaS in 20 minutes,' 'the neural network wrote me an app,' 'one prompt replaced a development team'... It all looks like the profession truly belongs in a museum next to punch cards and floppy disks, as now an ordinary internet user can conjure up enterprise software, a banking mobile app, and a taxi aggregator. And all this just in the morning. But the more I work with AI tools, the less I believe in the disappearance of developers. And not because AI is stupid. Quite the opposite – AI writes code well now. But to avoid discussing the topic abstractly, I'll tell you one illustrative story. I'll deliberately take the most modest scale possible: no backend, no Kafka, and no eight services. One frontend. To be completely honest, it will be one search screen. We'll see everything there. Read more

item.title: Kubernetes without Borders: Managed Kubernetes as a Computing Center for AI
item.description:
The evolution of artificial intelligence has reached a stage where downloading neural network weights from an open repository takes a few clicks, while implementing an algorithm into a production environment turns into a months-long quest. This gap is partly explained by the fact that traditional infrastructure is not flexible or adaptive enough for conditions where every minute of downtime translates into lost profit. It was this contradiction that catalyzed the transition to fundamentally new platforms. My name is Alexander Prokhorov. I am an expert in the Developer Productivity development team at VK Cloud. In this article, I will explain why classic infrastructure hindered the development of AI projects and what approach to managing computing resources has become the answer to these challenges. item.title: What Makes a Developer Valuable When AI Agents Are Getting Better at Writing Code
item.description:
Over the past year, I've found myself writing significantly less code manually and delegating much more to AI agents: implementation, tests, codebase exploration, option generation, and parts of analysis. This has prompted me to re-evaluate a rather simple hypothesis about the future of development. Initially, I believed that as AI capabilities grew, an engineer's value would simply shift from writing code to architecture and technical decision-making. I decided to test this idea. I reviewed studies on developer productivity with AI, engineering company career ladders, and spoke with Middle/Senior developers, Team Leads, and Engineering Managers. The picture turned out to be more complex. AI can indeed accelerate work significantly, but the effect depends on the task, experience, and context. Green tests don't guarantee a change is production-ready. And the ability to work with uncertainty doesn't, by itself, fully explain the difference between Middle and Senior levels. In this article, I explore what starts to better indicate an engineer's level in such an environment and why implementation itself is gradually becoming less convincing proof of good engineering work. item.title: VLM Hallucinations in Zero-Shot Detection: False Alarms about Smoke and a Prompt-Level Solution
item.description:
How I tried to solve the task of fire and smoke detection without training, using zero-shot detection on VLMs. I describe how it initially worked on videos with real smoke, but on clearly smoke-free streets, the model found "smoke" in 70% of my data: drawing bounding boxes on cars, signs, and traffic lights, sometimes with 0% confidence and a textual explanation that there was no smoke. The article explains why the one-step bbox format provokes false detections, which standard prompt engineering techniques didn't help, and what prompt change reduced the proportion of false alarms from 70% of frames to zero while maintaining over 80% recall. Read on.

item.title: If your developers use Claude Code, you haven't automated development yet
item.description:
Imagine hiring a confident mid-level developer for your team. But they weren't given access to the tracker, weren't shown the knowledge base, and were only told about architectural decisions once during onboarding. They are occasionally asked to Google something, sometimes assigned a small feature detached from the big picture, and then blamed for poor understanding of the task and company processes. This is roughly how I see the implementation of neural networks in development processes. Below, I'll discuss the pitfalls that arise when implementing agent-based development, regardless of team or company size, and what I've developed and observed from years of pair programming with computers. item.title: And Why Does Artificial Intelligence Need a Soul? A Philological Analysis of Nikita Mikhalkov's Manifesto
item.description:
Nikita Mikhalkov recently spoke about artificial intelligence, stating that if AI replaces humans, art will lose its meaning because machines lack conscience, soul, compassion, fear, or love. While agreeing that AI doesn't possess these human qualities, the author questions why it should. The article argues that AI is 'artificial intelligence,' not 'artificial human being,' and that the public discourse has mistakenly anthropomorphized AI, leading to fear over its lack of human traits. It proposes a collaborative model where AI acts as a creative partner, generating novel ideas through dialogue, rather than a replacement for human creators. The author concludes that the focus should be on the creative output of human-AI collaboration, not on whether AI has a soul, emphasizing that human creativity and responsibility remain paramount.
